blocks.heading: Ways to group activities
blocks.text: Businesses can group work by function, product, market or systems. Functional organisation groups similar activities, such as finance and marketing. Product organisation groups responsibility around different products or product ranges. Market organisation groups work around customer markets, which may be geographical areas or customer types. Systems organisation can use project-based teams bringing different skills together to complete a defined piece of work. These approaches answer different coordination needs and can be combined. A product division may still contain functional specialists. Grouping by function does not, by itself, establish whether decisions are centralised: finance staff can be grouped together while some spending authority is delegated elsewhere. The organisation should make reporting and responsibility clear so that coordination across groups does not become a dispute about who decides.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Taleni Manufacturing has both household furniture and school furniture ranges. It considers product teams instead of one shared production department. Product teams can focus on the different ranges and customer needs, but may duplicate specialist support. A functional structure pools that expertise, although the two product ranges then compete for its attention.

blocks.heading: Organisation by function
blocks.text: Organisation by function groups jobs and activities according to their role, such as production, finance, marketing or human resources. It pools specialist expertise and can clarify functional responsibility. However, departments may focus on their own targets and coordination between them can be difficult. Functional grouping is not a synonym for decentralisation; decision authority can be retained centrally or delegated.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Yela Goods groups all accounting staff in finance and all sales staff in marketing. These are functional departments. Whether their heads may approve spending depends on the authority granted, not simply their department names.

blocks.heading: Organisation by product
blocks.text: Organisation by product groups activities around a product or product range. A product head can coordinate the production and sales needs of that range, making responsibility for its performance clearer. Different divisions may duplicate support services, and resources can be contested between products. Use product grouping where distinct ranges need concentrated attention rather than assuming every product needs a separate division.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Alu Home has a bedding division and a cooking-equipment division. The grouping is by product range. A finance team within each division would be a function inside the product structure, not a different classification of the whole enterprise.

blocks.heading: Organisation by market
blocks.text: Organisation by market groups activity according to the market served, such as geographical areas or customer types. It can focus attention on different local or customer needs. Separate market units may duplicate activities and need common policy to protect consistency. A market-based structure does not prove that local heads have unlimited decision authority.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tula Supply has a northern-region unit and a southern-region unit; another supplier separates household and institutional customers. Both organise around markets, one geographical and one by customer type. Product grouping would instead divide the enterprise by the goods it supplies.

blocks.heading: Organisation by systems
blocks.text: Organisation by systems uses a project-based arrangement in which people with relevant skills work together on a defined project. A project team can coordinate contributions from different functions and focus on a shared result. Clear responsibility is needed where specialists also retain links to their functional departments. When the project ends, people may move to other work. This is an organisational arrangement, not simply installing computer software.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Eha Shelters draws a designer, purchasing officer and installation supervisor into a team for a school-shade project. The team coordinates a defined project rather than grouping everyone permanently by a single function. It needs agreed authority so project priorities and departmental requests do not conflict.
